content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
Summary:

The paper describes a new approach to high dimensiona BO using two key ingredients: 1) a deep kernel GP model with a transformer model specifying the deep kernel. 2) An acquistion function that is learned via a soft actor critic agent that uses the BO problem represented as a Markov decision process.  The proposed method shows some improvement over other BO benchmarks on several optimization problems.

Strengths:

- Important problem: BO where inputs are high-dimensional.
- Using transformer-based models to learn good features novel and potentially useful.
- Well-written paper.
- Successful results on different domains

Weaknesses:

- Deep kernel learning is known to overfit.
- High error bars in experimental section.
- Previous work on high-dimensional BO is not considered.
- the related work has not sufficiently covered the BO literature.
- Main claim supported only on artificial problems.

Recommendation:

This paper proposes a good concept for a deep learning based BO method.  However, it has not been properly justified and empirically demonstrated.  All reviewers vote for rejection. I therefore recommend rejection and encourage the authors to use the feedback provided by the reviewers to improve the paper.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: All reviewers vote for rejection and it is clear that the paper needs significant improvement before publication. There is a significant lack of review of previous related work. The experiments are not convincing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the problem of optimizing black-box functions via model based optimization (concretely Bayesian optimization). The proposed approach consists of two key components: (1) a deep kernel based surrogate model where a transformer is used for representation learning before being fed into a `combination kernel` (defined by truncating the feature space expansion series of the RBF kernel) and (2) an acquisition function which is learned via soft-actor critic agent by considering the BO problem as a Markov decision processs (MDP). An explicit exploration component is also added to the learned acquisition function.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- The paper considers an important problem where inputs are high-dimensional.
- The general idea of employing transformer based models to learn good features by passing a sequence of inputs is interesting and potentially useful for other model-based optimization techniques.

However, I have few questions and suggestions to understand some of the details better and that will hopefully improve the paper's contributions:

- The justification behind the combination kernel is not clear. Please describe why a standard RBF/Matern kernel is not employed directly? Why a truncation in the feature representation is required? How is the choice of K set to 5? 

- It is mentioned in the text that `...relying purely on the actor for selecting good actions while exploring performs poorly
on the small sample counts found in Bayesian optimization.` Is this a general statement about learned acquisition functions or is it an empirical statement about the proposed SAC based agent? 

- Recent works ([1], [2]) has shown overfitting and generalization issues with deep kernel learning (especially in the small data setting). Please discuss whether and how these issues affect the proposed approach. One way to test the surrogate model independently of the BO loop is to construct a standard train-test scenario and evaluate the model log-likelihood or mean squared error on the test set. 

- The variance of the error bars denoting the proposed approach in experimental section is quite high (please see Figure 3). Please describe the number of runs employed for showing these results. Why is the Asteriod 12-D results are cut in the y-axis below? Regarding Figure 1, it is mentioned that `... RTDK performs on par with other methods, showing very good performance on the higher dimensional PM2.5 data-set.` I don't think this is an accurate observation because multiple baselines outperform the proposed approach by a good enough margin on Oil-40D, HPOBench, Asteriod and Electric Grid. Please let me know if I am missing something here.

- There is a large body of work on high-dimensional Bayesian optimization (3-7) which is the most relevant to the proposed approach but unfortunately not discussed in the paper. Some of these works would serve as the right baseline for the high-dimensional problem setting. Please consider adding appropriate discussion/results comparing with these approaches.



[1] Ober, Sebastian W., Carl E. Rasmussen, and Mark van der Wilk. "The promises and pitfalls of deep kernel learning." In Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, pp. 1206-1216. PMLR, 2021.

[2] van Amersfoort, Joost, Lewis Smith, Andrew Jesson, Oscar Key, and Yarin Gal. "On feature collapse and deep kernel learning for single forward pass uncertainty." arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.11409 (2021).

[3] Eriksson, D., Pearce, M., Gardner, J., Turner, R. D., & Poloczek, M. (2019). Scalable global optimization via local bayesian optimization. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 32.

[4] Li, C., Gupta, S., Rana, S., Nguyen, V., Venkatesh, S., & Shilton, A. (2017). High Dimensional Bayesian Optimization Using Dropout. Proceedings of the 26th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 2096–2102. Melbourne, Australia: AAAI Press.

[5] Wang, Z., Gehring, C., Kohli, P., & Jegelka, S. (2018, March). Batched large-scale Bayesian optimization in high-dimensional spaces. In International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (pp. 745-754). PMLR.

[6] Oh, C., Gavves, E., & Welling, M. (2018, July). BOCK: Bayesian optimization with cylindrical kernels. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 3868-3877). PMLR.

[7] Eriksson, David, and Martin Jankowiak. "High-dimensional Bayesian optimization with sparse axis-aligned subspaces." In Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, pp. 493-503. PMLR, 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Some of the main components of the proposed approach (including the usage of transformer for bayesian inference) is already existing and employed directly without significant modification. The paper is written fairly well. Since there are many moving parts (transformer, deep kernel learning, soft-actor critic learned acquisition function), it seems essential to release the source code for robustly verifying the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper considers an important problem but many design choices are not justified and the experimental evaluation is slightly weak. Some relevant related work on high-dimensional Bayesian optimization is not discussed appropriately and the paper requires lot more work before acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors propose a new technique to combine recent approaches from deep kernel learning with transformer to improve GP modelling in meta-learning settings. Given this deep kernel, the authors then introduce a Gaussian process to model uncertainty and present an RL-like algorithm to learn acquisition values. In a set of experiments in various domains, the authors demonstrate that this method can yield favourable results. 

Although this paper is interesting and yields successful results, I am bit confused about the experimental section and the novelty of the approach. Please see below.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- New method combines transformers as `warping' functions with Bayesian optimisation. 
- Successful results on different domains 

Weaknesses: 
- I am a bit confused about the novelty of the proposed approach. If I understand correctly, this paper demonstrates that one can use transformer deep kernels to model and execute BO with an RL-like method. If that is the case, can the authors elaborate on why such an application is not trivial? What are the significant difficulties faced when executing this approach? It has not been clear to me when reading the paper what the major challenges are. Maybe the authors could rewrite significant parts of the paper emphasising the novelty of the approach. As it stands, this paper looks to be an application-like manuscript. That is acceptable, but if that is the case, some novelty claims must be addressed. 
- In Figure 3, the authors demonstrate various results of the proposed technique compared to some benchmarks. I am a bit worried about why the variance of RTDK is very high. Does it seem that the regret varies anywhere from the best to the worst performing method? 
- I am not convinced about the claim of high dimensionality presented in this paper. There is a significant amount of literature tackling high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation that has been ignored in this manuscript. Those include problems that perform projection-based learning followed by BO in latent spaces. In these papers, molecular design ( a high-d prob) is generally used and benchmarked. I urge the authors to at least reference those works and run a comparison to those methods on one of those domains. Similarly, this goes to multi-objective Bayesian optimisation. Many works perform that but are not referenced in the paper. 
- Finally, a more general comment related to the approach of meta-Bayesian optimisation. Are we saying that now we are not interested in black-box optimisation anymore? Since if we do a meta-setting, we somehow assume similarities to the target domain. If that is the case, don't we somehow assume we know the target domain?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As mentioned in the previous section of this review, the paper can improve in quality and novelty. Reading this paper left me with more questions than answers. As for novelty, please refer to the previous set of comments.
content.summary_of_the_review: In short, I think this paper is interesting. However, at this stage, I am not convinced of the novelty and experimental sections. I hope the authors can help me understand during the rebuttal phase.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new high dimensional BO approach using deep architectures and reinforcement learning. There are two key ideas. The surrogate GP is parameterized by a transformer architecture. The acquisition function is replaced by a soft actor critic component. The proposed method shows some improvement over other BO benchmarks on several optimization problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: The idea is relatively novel and interesting. 

Weakness: 

Regarding clarity:
-- The introduction is extremely brief and fails to highlight the high level idea behind the proposal. For example, this does not seem like a good motivation -- "In this work, we aim to improve Bayesian Optimization’s generalizability and sample efficiency by introducing deep learning methods into both these components", nor do the following two sentences, which describe the methods without providing any concrete justification regarding why they should work.

-- I think the related work has not sufficiently covered the BO literature. Despite the claim on the paper title being high-dim BO, there is not a single high-dim BO being mentioned in section 2. The literature review on deep learning based BO is also missing many. The paper only reviews FSAF and MetaBO, which are by no means representative of the field. Some example citations:
Bayesian Optimization in a Billion Dimensions via Random Embeddings, Wang et al., 2013
Scalable Bayesian Optimization Using Deep Neural Networks, Snoek et al, 2015
Batched High-dimensional Bayesian Optimization via Structural Kernel Learning, Wang et al., 2017
High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimisation with Variational Autoencoders and Deep Metric Learning, Grosnit et al., 2021

-- (minor) I think the technical details of soft actor critic and transformer should be summarized to make the paper self-contained.

Regarding quality:

-- The RBF kernel has a closed form. The infinite sum is basically the expansion of the exponential function. Why do we need to approximate it via truncation in Eq (1)? 
-- " However, if we believe that our actor generally learns the landscape of our Q-function, then we can sample from the actor in order to assist with generating samples from the Boltzmann Q using importance sampling" --- this description is vague and sounds like a contradiction to the previous statement "we find that relying purely on the actor for selecting good actions while exploring performs poorly
on the small sample counts found in Bayesian optimization" (which suggests that the actor can be inaccurate). Can the authors clarify the meaning of these statements? 

-- "In general, each trajectory may originate from a different underlying objective. This enables meta learning between similar objectives as both the agent and model must perform well across many different trajectories." --- What are the different objectives here? I thought the samples on these trajectories belong to the same black-box function? I also do not get the overall point about meta learning. As far as I understand, meta learning typically means generalizing across tasks -- none of the experiments seems to demonstrate such a setting.

-- Regarding section 6.1, it is great that RTDK can perform on discrete baselines, but why is this relevant to the claims of this paper (e.g., being high-dimensional and improve generalizability). I also don't think the performance is competitive as claimed, seeing that it loses to the majority of baselines in most experiments and has a huge variance.

-- Regarding section 6.2, EI, PI and UCB are not really high-dim BO methods. The proposed method should be compared against more appropriate baselines.

-- I think Cumulative/Average regret is a more common metric than Median regret. Is there a reason for this choice of metric?

-- Why does RTDK always have a spike in median regret around 50 function samples for all Thompson regardless of the dimension? 

-- (minor) Fig 5c is cut off. y-axis should extend to at least 10 to properly show the regret on Thompson 64D.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is not well written. Introduction and related work are insufficient. Most key ideas are unsubstantiated.

Quality: The proposed method is not compared to appropriate benchmarks. Section 6.1 doesn't seem like good results to me. 

Novelty: The combination of RL and Transformer GP is novel. Some practical techniques to improve RL in this particular use case also seem novel. 

Reproducibility: No supplementary code nor anonymous github repo was provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend a rejection. This paper proposes a good concept for a deep learning based BO method. However, it has not been properly justified and empirically demonstrated.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors develop a new surrogate model which uses a deep kernel using a transformer encoder/decoder architecture combined with what the authors call a combination kernel. Furthermore, they use a model-based soft actor-critic to obtain an acquisition function. The method is evaluation on different problems with varying dimensionalities.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:** The solution sounds very interesting.

**Weaknesses:**
1. Paper is clear in many aspects.
- Please provide hyperparameters used and how they were estimated, how you train your model and on what data and do you update it during the optimization. What is the exact experimental setup and provide more details on the benchmarks.
2. Reason for certain design choices are not provided.
- Why use SAC of Q-Learning, what's the purpose of the ocmbination kernel, why not use EI/UCB (more questions below)?
3. Main claim supported only on artificial problems
- Use a high-dimensional problem where a single function evaluation is expensive.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work combines the concepts of existing works, i.e., transformer kernels and RL acquisition functions.

The authors’ main claim is that their method improves in high dimensional continuous domains. This claim is supported in experiments on the Powell function minimization and Thomson problem solving. It is unclear why these are representative high-dimensional problems that require to be solved sample-efficiently. Evaluating a single configuration is very cheap and limiting the number of trials to at most 150 is unreasonable. Given that the simple baselines are already on par for this small budget, I don’t see the complexity of this method justified.

On lower-dimensional problems, the authors do not report any improvement.

The paper has many unclarities. Neither the experimental setup, nor the own method and its training, nor the benchmarks are sufficiently described.

The proposed solution is incredibly complex and not all hyperparameters are made public nor do the authors discuss how one would fine these hyperparameters for a new problem.

It is unclear how the surrogate is trained and on which data. The authors mention in 6.1 that 250 function samples are used for pre-training. From which function are these samples?

The ablation study lacks important experiments justifying the made decisions. The proposed method is very similar to FSAF. How does it compare against SAC-FSAF? How does the proposed work with Q-Learning instead of SAC? How does it compare against FSAF with transformer? What’s the reason to combine the transformer with the combination kernel? Is it necessary to use this special acquisition function? How does it compare against the surrogate with transformer kernel + EI/UCB? The only ablation in that direction answers the question whether a transformer kernel is justified and the answer seems to be no.

Minor remarks:

The authors refer for to the appendix of the FSAF paper for explanation of their own experimental setup. The paper should be self-contained in my opinion.

The authors report the regret for the Thomson problem which isn’t well-defined given that the optimum is unknown.

The abbreviation RTDK was never introduced. It appears that the method was inconsistently renamed to TDKL.

For the experiments reported in Figure 4, the authors noted that some methods are optimized on a discrete grid. All these methods perform equally bad. Is the grid chosen too small? The authors argued that this change was necessary because adapting these methods to the continuous domain is challenging. May the authors want to elaborate that? I understand it for MetaBO because this is required here. However, I don’t recall that the other methods need it, e.g., MES and TAF. On that note, the results for TAF are only shown in the first plot of Figure 4. Why is it missing for the other 2 plots?

The problem is called Thomson problem (no p).
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors present an interesting idea but are not able to demonstrate its usefulness in a relevant application. Many important details are missing which makes understanding or reproducing the results very difficult. Important ablations are missing to justify important design choices which differ from other works.

content.title: High Dimensional Bayesian Optimization with Reinforced Transformer Deep Kernels
content.TL;DR: Transformer Deep Kernels combined with general combination gaussian process kernels help optimize high dimensional functions when using reinforcement learning acquisitions for exploration.
content.abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) has proved to be an invaluable technique for efficient, high-dimensional optimization. The use of Gaussian process (GP) surrogates and dynamic acquisition functions has allowed BO to shine in challenging high dimensional optimization due to its sample efficiency and uncertainty modeling. Reinforcement Learning has been introduced to improve optimization performance on both single function optimization as well as \textit{few-shot} multi-objective optimization. However, until now, even few-shot techniques treat each objective as independent optimization tasks, failing to exploit the similarities shared between objectives. We combine recent developments in Deep Kernel Learning (DKL) and attention-based Transformer models to improve the modeling powers of GP surrogates with meta-learning. We propose a method for improving meta-learning BO surrogates by incorporating attention mechanisms into DKL, empowering the surrogates to adapt to contextual information gathered during the BO process. This Transformer Deep Kernel is combined with Reinforcement Learning techniques to aid in exploration, ensuring state-of-the-art results on a variety of high-dimensional optimization problems.
